practice1.prompt: write a test suite for find_max that catches all three seeded bugs

cases.name: your tests pass the working version and catch all three bugs

practice1.hint: The starter test already catches two of the three. The one still standing is about the list with nothing in it: decide what find_max should do with [] and assert it.

questions.prompt: What does a test suite that goes green actually tell you?
choices: The code passes the cases you thought to write
questions.explain: Green means nothing you asked about was wrong. A bug in a case you never wrote is a bug your suite is silent about, which is why the cases you choose are the whole of the work.

questions.prompt: Which of these are worth a test of their own for a function that finds the largest number?
choices: A list where the largest is at the end
The same list tested three times
questions.explain: Each of the first three can break independently. Repeating one list three times triples the running time and tests exactly as much as running it once.

questions.prompt: Why is a test that says assert True worth nothing?
choices: It passes whether the code works or not, so it can never report a bug
questions.explain: A test earns its place by being able to fail. One that passes against every version of a function, working or broken, has no opinion about the code at all.

questions.prompt: A test that cannot ___ cannot tell you anything when it passes.
questions.explain: Passing is only informative next to the possibility of failing. That is the whole reason a suite is judged on the bugs it catches rather than on its colour.
